title: The Stone Hills
subtitle: Göbekli Tepe, Karahan Tepe and the Taş Tepeler
era: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and early B
summary: On limestone ridges around Şanlıurfa, people who still hunted and gathered carved and raised stone pillars more than 11,000 years ago. Göbekli Tepe and its newly excavated neighbours have overturned old ideas about what came first, monuments or farms, and the answer is still being rewritten.
narration: Some 600 kilometres north of the Natufian hamlets, on a bare limestone ridge above the plain of Şanlıurfa in southeastern Türkiye, farmers had long been dragging broken slabs of stone out of their fields. Surveyors who visited in 1963 took them for medieval gravestones. In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt saw something else: the heads of carved pillars, each shaped like a giant letter T.

Under the hill lay round enclosures ringed with pillars, the tallest about five and a half metres high, raised around 11,500 years ago. Foxes snarl across their faces, snakes stream down their sides, vultures spread their wings. The two central pillars of one enclosure have arms carved along their flanks, hands meeting above a belt, and a fox pelt hanging as a loincloth. They are not just stones. They are beings.

Schmidt believed he had found a mountain sanctuary built by hunter-gatherers, a temple that came before the town and perhaps nudged people toward farming. The researchers who followed him have found rain cisterns, houses and thousands of grinding stones, and a dozen neighbouring hills, the Taş Tepeler, are now yielding carved heads, leopards and whole rooms cut from the living rock. The builders still hunted gazelle and harvested wild grain. What they made has changed how we picture the people who lived on the eve of farming.

body.heading: A hill of pillars
paragraphs: Göbekli Tepe (“potbelly hill” in Turkish) is an artificial mound about 15 m high and some 300 m across on a limestone ridge about 15 km northeast of Şanlıurfa. A joint survey by the universities of Istanbul and Chicago recorded it in 1963 as a Neolithic site littered with flint, but took the broken limestone slabs on its surface for medieval graves. In 1994 Klaus Schmidt of the German Archaeological Institute (DAI), who had worked at the nearby site of Nevalı Çori, recognised the slabs as the tops of T-shaped pillars. Excavations with the Şanlıurfa Museum began in 1995.

The older level, Layer III, holds large round or oval enclosures. Four of them, labelled A to D, have been excavated, and geophysical surveys suggest more beneath the mound. Each has ten or more pillars set into a stone wall with benches, facing two taller central pillars. In Enclosure D, about 20 m across, the central pillars stand some 5.5 m high and weigh several tonnes each. A quarry on the plateau still holds an unfinished pillar nearly 7 m long. The younger Layer II consists of smaller rectangular rooms with smaller pillars, often only one or two.

body.heading: Beasts and beings in stone
paragraphs: Carved in relief on the pillars are foxes, wild boars, snakes, aurochs, wild asses, cranes, vultures, scorpions and spiders. Gazelle, the animal most often eaten at the site, barely appears, so the imagery is not a menu but a selection, perhaps of dangerous or symbolically charged creatures. Individual enclosures seem to favour particular animals: snakes in A, foxes in B, boars in C. On Pillar 43 in Enclosure D, the so-called Vulture Stone, a vulture spreads its wings beside a disc, above a scorpion and a headless figure.

The central pillars of Enclosure D are more than posts. Arms run down their sides, long-fingered hands meet above a belt, and a fox pelt hangs from the belt like a loincloth; the T-shaped top is a stylised head. Schmidt read them as supernatural beings or ancestors. Free-standing sculptures add human heads, animals and a pole of stacked figures. In 2023 the excavators announced a life-size limestone boar from Enclosure D, 1.35 m long, which still carried red, black and white pigment, the first painted sculpture known from the period. It stood on a bench carved with an H-shaped sign, a crescent, snakes and three human faces. In 2025 a statue of a human with a clearly shaped head and torso turned up, reused and laid horizontally, in a wall between Enclosures B and D.

body.heading: Dating and filling
paragraphs: Radiocarbon dates place the Layer III enclosures in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA), roughly 9500 to 8800 BCE, and the Layer II buildings in the early and middle Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB), down to about 8000 BCE. The dates are harder to pin down than they sound. The enclosures were filled with rubble, flint, bone and soil, so charcoal and bone inside them can be older or younger than the walls, and the team has also dated organic material trapped in wall plaster.

Schmidt believed the enclosures had been deliberately buried when their use ended, which would explain their fine preservation. Research since his death in 2014, led by Lee Clare of the DAI with Oliver Dietrich, Jens Notroff, Moritz Kinzel and Turkish colleagues, suggests a messier history: enclosures were rebuilt and modified over centuries, and slope slides from higher parts of the mound helped fill them. Some team members think the enclosures may have been roofed, a question that remains open.

body.heading: From sanctuary to settlement
paragraphs: Schmidt’s interpretation was bold. Göbekli Tepe, he argued, was a hilltop sanctuary without houses or a spring, where scattered bands of hunter-gatherers came together to build and worship. “First came the temple, then the city,” he said. Feeding the workforce might have encouraged intensive harvesting of wild cereals, and a 1997 genetic study by Manfred Heun and colleagues had traced domestic einkorn wheat to the nearby Karacadağ hills.

The team that followed him has reshaped that picture. Excavations since about 2014 have found rock-cut cisterns and channels that collected rainwater, domestic buildings, hearths and more than 7,000 grinding slabs, handstones, mortars and pestles. A 2019 study led by Laura Dietrich combined use-wear, plant phytoliths and animal bones: wild cereals were ground on a large scale, and gazelle were hunted in bulk between midsummer and autumn. Because no large storage facilities have been found, the authors proposed seasonal work feasts. Big limestone vessels, some holding up to about 160 litres, may have held fermented drinks, though that remains speculative.

Every plant and animal identified at Göbekli Tepe so far is wild. Lee Clare has said he does not see the site as the “smoking gun” of the Neolithic, but rather as a monumental effort by hunter-gatherers facing a changing world. The Canadian archaeologist Edward Banning had argued in 2011 that the sharp line between temple and house is a modern one, and in 2023 he reviewed a decade of reinterpretation under the title “Paradise found or common sense lost?”

body.heading: Carved skulls
paragraphs: No graves have been found, but hundreds of fragments of human bone have, most of them from skulls. In 2017 Julia Gresky, Juliane Haelm and Lee Clare described three skull pieces with deep grooves cut along the top with flint tools, one also drilled with a hole, all bearing cut marks from defleshing. The grooves may have held cords so the skulls could be hung up or decorated. It was a form of skull cult not seen before, a local variant of the Neolithic attention to heads that appears in the plastered skulls of the Levant (chapter 33).

body.heading: A landscape of stone hills
paragraphs: Göbekli Tepe was never alone. At Nevalı Çori, excavated by Harald Hauptmann from 1983 to 1991 before the Atatürk Dam reservoir flooded it in 1992, T-shaped pillars and sculptures stood in a special building inside an ordinary village of rectangular houses. At Körtik Tepe on the upper Tigris, hundreds of PPNA burials were furnished with finely carved stone bowls. Since 2021 the Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism has run the Taş Tepeler (“stone hills”) project, with excavations at a dozen sites in Şanlıurfa province.

The most spectacular is Karahan Tepe, about 46 km east of Göbekli Tepe, excavated by Necmi Karul of Istanbul University. Its builders carved rooms out of the bedrock. In one, Structure AB, ten pillars shaped as phalluses rise from the rock floor while a human head on a long neck projects from the wall above them. Finds announced in recent seasons include a man carrying a leopard on his back, a 2.3 m statue of a seated man holding his phallus and, in August 2026, a 70 cm sculpture of a person sitting on a leopard’s back.

At Sayburç, near Şanlıurfa, Eylem Özdoğan excavated a rock-cut communal building whose bench carries a relief of two scenes: a man holding his phallus between two leopards, and a man with a rattle or snake facing a bull. Published in 2022, it is among the oldest narrative scenes in art. Harbetsuvan Tepesi has produced a seated male statue, and at Sefer Tepe, where the tops of about 16 T-shaped pillars show through the soil, two carved human faces were announced in 2025. The emerging picture is of a whole region of villages with special buildings, sharing a symbolic world of men, predators and the dead.

body.heading: Comets, calendars and lost civilisations
paragraphs: Göbekli Tepe’s fame has invited bolder readings. In 2017 the chemical engineer Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis argued that the animals on the Vulture Stone are constellations recording a comet impact around 10,950 BCE, part of the contested Younger Dryas impact hypothesis. In 2024, in the journal Time and Mind, Sweatman read V-shaped marks on the same pillar as a calendar of 365 days: twelve lunar months plus eleven extra days. The excavators and most archaeologists reject both claims (see Debates).

The site is also a favourite of pseudo-archaeology. Graham Hancock’s books and his 2022 Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse present it as the legacy of a lost, advanced Ice Age civilisation. Nothing found there supports that: the tools are flint and bone, the food is wild, and earlier villages such as Hallan Çemi and Körtik Tepe show the culture’s local roots. What the evidence does show is remarkable enough: people who lived by hunting and gathering could plan, quarry, carve and gather in numbers on a scale once thought to require farming.

debates.question: Was Göbekli Tepe a sanctuary or a settlement?

views.label: A ritual centre
views.text: Klaus Schmidt (1953–2014) argued that Göbekli Tepe was a mountain sanctuary without permanent houses, where dispersed hunter-gatherer groups met to build, feast and worship. He pointed to the lack of obvious dwellings in the early excavations, the absence of a spring, the figurative pillars as supernatural beings, and what he saw as the deliberate burial of the enclosures.

views.label: A settlement with special buildings
views.text: Since 2014 Lee Clare, Moritz Kinzel, Oliver Dietrich and colleagues have reported domestic buildings, rock-cut cisterns and water channels, more than 7,000 grinding tools and abundant flint-knapping waste, all signs of people living on the site. Edward Banning argued as early as 2011 that separating ‘temples’ from ‘houses’ imposes a modern distinction on Neolithic buildings that could be both.

debates.status: Most specialists now accept that people lived at Göbekli Tepe for long periods and that the enclosures were special communal buildings within a settlement, much like those at Nevalı Çori and Karahan Tepe. How many people lived there, whether the enclosures were roofed, and whether they were buried deliberately or filled by slope slides and rebuilding are still argued.

debates.question: Did monument building drive the invention of farming?

views.label: Temple first
views.text: Schmidt suggested that the need to feed large work parties and gatherings encouraged intensive harvesting and eventually cultivation of wild cereals, noting that einkorn wheat was domesticated in the nearby Karacadağ hills. The idea echoes Jacques Cauvin’s argument that a change in beliefs preceded farming.

views.label: Feasting hunter-gatherers
views.text: The current team stresses that every plant and animal identified at Göbekli Tepe is wild, that gazelle hunting dominated, and that grinding and feasting were part of a hunter-gatherer economy. Lee Clare has described the monuments as a response by hunter-gatherers to social and environmental change rather than the trigger of farming, which emerged slowly across the whole Fertile Crescent (chapter 33).

debates.status: No domesticated plants or animals have been identified at Göbekli Tepe. Most researchers now treat monument building, feasting and the slow shift to cultivation as parts of one long transformation, in which communal work and ritual helped create the social ties that settled life needed, rather than one simply causing the other.

debates.question: Do the carvings record a comet and a calendar?

views.label: An astronomical code
views.text: Martin Sweatman of the University of Edinburgh, with Dimitrios Tsikritsis (2017), matched animals on Pillar 43 to constellations and derived a date of about 10,950 BCE, which he links to a proposed comet impact at the start of the Younger Dryas. In a 2024 paper in Time and Mind he interpreted V-shaped marks as a 365-day lunisolar calendar and extended the reading to Karahan Tepe.

views.label: Local symbolism
views.text: The excavators, in a 2017 reply by Jens Notroff, Oliver Dietrich, Lee Clare and colleagues, pointed out that Enclosure D was built more than a thousand years after the supposed event, that the same animals recur across the region’s iconography, that linking them to much later Greek or Mesopotamian constellations is arbitrary, and that the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis itself is rejected by most specialists. Counting V-signs as days, critics add, depends on selective choices.

debates.status: The astronomical readings have little support among archaeologists who work on the site or the period, although they circulate widely in popular books and online. A convincing case would need predictions tested against the whole corpus of carvings rather than one selected pillar.

sites.name: Göbekli Tepe
sites.summary: Mound with monumental enclosures of carved T-shaped pillars up to 5.5 m high, built by hunter-gatherers. Recent work has added cisterns, domestic buildings, thousands of grinding tools, grooved skulls and a painted boar statue.

sites.name: Karahan Tepe
sites.summary: Taş Tepeler site with rooms carved from bedrock, including a chamber of ten phallic pillars watched by a human head emerging from the wall. Statues include a seated man 2.3 m tall and, found in 2026, a person riding a leopard.

sites.name: Nevalı Çori
sites.summary: Early PPNB village where T-shaped pillars and sculptures were first recognised, in a special building among rectangular houses. Excavated 1983–1991 by Harald Hauptmann, it now lies beneath the Atatürk Dam reservoir.

sites.name: Sayburç
sites.summary: Village with a rock-cut communal building whose bench bears reliefs of a man between two leopards and a man facing a bull, published in 2022 as one of the oldest narrative scenes known.

sites.name: Körtik Tepe
sites.summary: Early village on the upper Tigris with hundreds of burials accompanied by decorated stone vessels, showing the local hunter-gatherer roots of the symbolic world seen at Göbekli Tepe.
